text.p: Pakistan on Thursday dismissed fears voiced in the United States and India about its alleged missile development, saying it was doing nothing contrary to its commitments.

A Foreign Ministry spokesman denied a Time magazine report saying the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) had located a facility at Rawalpindi, near Islamabad, that could make Chinese M-11 missiles.
"The agency concluded that not only was China selling missiles, but it was also helping Pakistan build a factory to manufacture them," Time's June 30 edition said.
"These reports are totally baseless, there is no foundation to them at all," the Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesman told reporters at a weekly news briefing.
"Rawalpindi is within walking distance of all of you and you are welcome to go and locate this particular factory," he said.
India's Defence Ministry signalled it would act in response to the alleged missile development.

"We are aware of outside assistance to Pakistan in this field despite the existence of multilateral export control regimes, unilateral declarations of restraint and supply restrictions in producer countries," it said in a statement issued in New Delhi.
"India will draw appropriate conclusions from these developments and remains prepared to safeguard the country's security against all eventualities."
The Washington Post, quoting a CIA report to Congress, said on Wednesday that China provided "a tremendous variety of assistance" to ballistic missile programmes in Iran and Pakistan.
The ministry spokesman said he had not studied this report.

"But I wish to assure you that Paksitan's cooperation with China is totally in the sphere of peaceful uses of these technologies. Pakistan is not engaged in any cooperation with any country that amounts to a violation of the understandings it has reached."
He dismissed concern expressed by the Indian Foreign Ministry on Wednesday over reports that Pakistan had test-fired a medium-range missile.

He confirmed a report in local newspapers that Pakistan's Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO) had test-fired a Hatf-series missile but said it was part of the commission's research for peaceful uses.
"SUPARCO is engaged in peaceful research and development of rocket motor technology...(and) carries out, from time to time, routine tests of rockets," he said.

The Nation newspaper said on Wednesday that Pakistani experts had successfully test-fired a Hatf-III missile with a range of 800 km (500 miles) compared to the 1,000-km (620-mile) and 200-km (125-mile) ranges of the previous Hatf-I and Hatf-II.

The spokesman did not confirm the range of the missile but said: "SUPARCO is a civilian organisation and all its activities are geared towards the civilian sector. There is no military component to it."

Pakistan, which has fought three wars with India since independence from British rule in 1947, criticises New Delhi for its plans to develop and test ballistic missiles, particularly the medium-range Prithvi.
India has been testing the Prithvi but New Delhi last month denied that such missiles had been deployed near the Pakistan border.
